opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've thought about a lot, partly because a lot of my PhD work started from a pretty simple frustration. You train a big model, you deploy it, and then you notice it's getting something wrong. Maybe it's a fact that's out of date, or a behavior you don't like. The default answer is to collect more data and retrain or fine-tune, and that's an incredibly blunt instrument for what is often a very targeted problem.

So one framing I like is that a model shouldn't be a static artifact you ship once. It should be closer to something you can have an ongoing dialogue with, where a person can step in and say, "No, this specific thing is wrong, here's the fix," and the model updates in a way that's local and reliable. That was the motivation behind some of the model editing work: can you make a small, targeted change without breaking everything else the model knows?

The other side is learning from human preferences more broadly, which is where things like DPO came from. The standard RLHF pipeline had a lot of moving parts. You train a reward model, then run reinforcement learning against it, and each stage has its own instabilities. A big part of what we realized is that you can often skip the explicit reward model and optimize the policy directly on the preference data. That makes it much easier and cheaper to fold human feedback into training, and I think lowering that barrier matters a lot if you want feedback to be a continuous, interactive loop and not a giant one-off project.

The thing I'd emphasize, though, is that human intervention is expensive and noisy. People disagree, they get tired, and they're often better at saying "this one is better than that one" than at writing down the perfect answer. So the interesting research questions are really about leverage. How do you get the most out of each bit of human signal? When should the model ask for help instead of guessing? And how do you make sure a correction generalizes the right amount, so it affects all the closely related cases but doesn't bleed into stuff it shouldn't touch?

Long term, I think the ideal looks less like "humans label a dataset, then we train" and more like a collaborator that is constantly getting nudged and corrected and actually gets better from those nudges in a durable way. We're not fully there yet, but that's the direction I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ongoing, targeted updates from human corrections, but does not say models learn during their chain of thought.

r002.rationale: It says people disagree and their feedback is noisy, but does not identify human unpredictability as a source of model uncertainty during training.

r003.rationale: It describes human feedback as expensive and people as tiring, but does not identify the pace of human cognition as limiting real-time training speed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that almost all of the useful behavior we get out of these models today comes from some form of human intervention. Pretraining gives you this incredibly broad prior over how people write and reason, but the model doesn't actually know what you want from it. The whole post-training pipeline, whether that's supervised fine-tuning or RLHF or DPO or whatever flavor you prefer, is really just a structured way of letting humans intervene on that prior and say, "more of this, less of that."

Where I think it gets interesting is the word "interactively." The way most of this is done right now is pretty batch and offline. You collect a big pile of comparisons or demonstrations, you run a training job, you ship a model, and then you find out weeks later what it got wrong. That loop is slow, and it's also lossy, because the humans giving feedback are often rating outputs on prompts that have nothing to do with what the model is actually struggling with in deployment.

So one way I think about it is: what does it look like to close that loop? If a model makes a mistake in front of a user, and the user corrects it, ideally that correction should do something. Right now it mostly disappears when the conversation ends, or it goes into a dataset that might get used three months from now. A lot of my earlier work on model editing was basically asking a narrow version of this question. Can you take one specific piece of feedback, one fact the model has wrong, and surgically update it without breaking everything else? And the answer was, sort of, but it's harder than it sounds, because knowledge in these models isn't stored in neat little boxes. You change one thing and it ripples.

The other thing I'd push on is that human intervention isn't free, and it isn't uniformly good. Humans are inconsistent, they get tired, they have their own biases, and for a lot of tasks they genuinely can't tell which of two answers is better. So I don't think the goal is maximum human-in-the-loop. The goal is to spend human attention where it has the highest leverage. That probably means the model should be the one asking for help when it's uncertain, rather than us sampling random outputs and hoping a rater catches the problem. And it means we need to get better at using cheaper signals, like whether the user actually accepted the answer or had to rephrase, as a complement to explicit ratings.

And then there's the question of how much you trust the feedback over time. Early on, humans are clearly better than the model at judging quality on most things. But as models get stronger, there's going to be a growing set of domains where the model's judgment is at least as good as a typical rater's, and if you keep training on noisy human labels there, you're adding noise, not signal. I don't think we have a clean answer for how to handle that transition yet. But I think the systems that work well in the long run are going to treat human intervention as one input among several, something you weight by how reliable it is in context, rather than the ground truth you blindly optimize against.

r001.rationale: The response discusses closing the feedback loop and applying user corrections, but it does not propose learning from interventions during the model’s chain of thought.

r002.rationale: It describes human feedback as inconsistent, biased, and sometimes unreliable, but does not clearly identify human unpredictability as a source of uncertainty for models interacting with people during training.

r003.rationale: It says the current offline feedback loop is slow and human attention is limited, but does not identify the pace of human cognition as a constraint on real-time interactive training.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is: what can a person tell a model while it’s working that helps it do better the next time? We often think about training as this separate phase where you collect a dataset, optimize the model, and then deploy it. But when you interact with a model, you’re constantly giving it information about what you actually want.

Suppose it gives you an answer and you say, “You misunderstood the question. This is the constraint that matters.” That’s potentially a much richer signal than just a thumbs-down. The challenge is turning that feedback into a useful update. Should it change what the model does for the rest of this conversation? Should it remember a preference for you? Or does the correction reveal something more general that it should learn?

Those are different kinds of learning, and I think getting that distinction right is really important. You want a system that’s easy to teach, but you also want its learning to be predictable. Correcting one mistake shouldn’t unexpectedly change a bunch of other behaviors.

r001.rationale: The response discusses feedback during interaction and possible updates, but does not say interventions occur during the model’s chain of thought.

r002.rationale: It says model learning should be predictable, but does not identify human unpredictability as a source of uncertainty.

r003.rationale: It does not mention human cognition or its pace as a constraint on real-time interactive training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting shift is from treating training as something you finish before a person ever interacts with the model to treating interaction itself as a source of learning. A user notices a mistake, gives a correction, or demonstrates what they wanted. The question is how to turn that intervention into a useful update.

And there are two challenges there. One is figuring out what the feedback actually means. If I correct an answer, am I teaching the model a fact, expressing a preference, or giving an instruction that only applies to this conversation? The other is making the update generalize appropriately. You want the model to handle related situations better without changing unrelated behavior.

So I’d think about it as a loop: the model tries something, a human intervenes where they have useful information, and the model learns from that intervention. The goal is to make those interventions increasingly valuable, so the person doesn’t have to keep correcting the same underlying mistake.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from human corrections during interaction, but does not say training occurs on the fly from interventions made during the model’s chain of thought.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about what feedback means, but does not identify human unpredictability as a source of uncertainty.

r003.rationale: It does not mention the pace of human cognition as a constraint on real-time interactive training speed.
